standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Invoked inside the counted proof (source lines 5244-5245)
standard_prerequisites.use: Shows that the new path survives the removal and the join operations.

core_obligations: Reduction: it suffices to treat the zig case, the zag case being the same argument (proof line 5236)

Type I: the new path is a zigzag path of the intermediate model, and the only zigzag paths meeting it do so exactly once in each deformed part with opposite directions, so it is type I and has no self-intersections (proof lines 5238-5243)

Survival of the operations: the edges of the new path are not removed, and the join operation does not affect it because it contains no two-valent node, so it persists in the deformed model and the remaining assertions follow from its definition (proof lines 5244-5246)
proof_roadmap: Treat the zig case; the zag case is similar.

z_{i,j} is a zigzag path of the intermediate model by definition; the zigzag paths meeting it are the ones described in the observations on deformed parts, meeting it exactly once per deformed part in prescribed directions, so it is type I and free of self-intersections.

Hence its edges are not removed by the removal operation, and because it contains no two-valent node the join operation does not affect it; so it is a type I zigzag path of the deformed model, and the class and length assertions follow from the definition of z_{i,j}.

The proof (source lines 5235-5247) restricts to the zig case, uses the description of the paths meeting the deformed part to establish the type I property and absence of self-intersections, and then checks that the path survives the removal and join operations (proof lines 5244-5246). The survival argument is the substance. H2.

core_obligations: Reduction: it suffices to treat the zig case, the zag case being the same argument (proof line 5260)

Class and survival: the construction makes the homology class equal to the original one, consistency rules out pathological behaviour on the irrelevant parts, and the intersections with the paths created by the deformation occur at most once in each direction, so the edges are not removed; the join operation only changes slopes, so the path survives as a path of the deformed model and is determined uniquely (proof lines 5267-5272)

Construct y'_k: coincide with y_k on all irrelevant parts and follow the prescribed local picture in each deformed part; it has no self-intersections and extends to the universal cover of the intermediate model, and by construction [y_k] = [y'_k].

Consistency prevents pathological behaviour on the irrelevant parts; the intersections with the paths z_{i,j} and x'_j happen at most once per direction, so no edge is removed; the join operation only changes slopes; hence y'_k survives to the deformed model and is unique.

This gives the first displayed equation; the inequality and the equality case follow from it and the description of P_i.

standard_prerequisites.name: The left to right crossing convention for zigzag paths on the universal cover
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Used inside the counted proof, which refers to the definition of zigzag paths (source line 1184)
standard_prerequisites.use: Fixes the two possible directions in which a lifting can cross the lifted path.

core_obligations: Contradiction setup: assume two intersection edges of which one is a zig and the other a zag of the type I path, choose liftings of both paths to the universal cover crossing the lifted type I path exactly at those liftings of the edges, and note that the lifted type I path separates the plane into two sides which the two liftings cross in opposite directions (proof lines 1177-1184)

Covering argument: the two liftings cross from opposite sides, so no translation can superimpose them, which contradicts the fact that both project to the same path on the surface (that is, contradicts the choice of the two liftings) (proof lines 1234-1236)
Conclusion: the assumed configuration is impossible, so the intersections of the path with the type I path lie entirely in the zigs or entirely in the zags (proof lines 1172-1174 with 1236)
proof_roadmap: Assume the intersections contain a zig e_1 and a zag e_2 of the type I path z, and lift both edges and the path w to the universal cover; the liftings w_1 and w_2 cross the lifted z exactly at those two lifted edges, and by the definition of zigzag paths they cross z from opposite sides (the author's figure illustrates this).
Since z is type I, the lifted paths w_1 and w_2 meet z only at those liftings of e_1 and e_2, so no translation of the plane can superimpose them.
Both liftings project to the same path w on the surface, so a deck transformation would have to superimpose them, a contradiction; hence the intersections cannot contain both a zig and a zag.

The proof (source lines 1177-1237) assumes two intersection edges of opposite type, lifts the configuration to the universal cover where the type I path separates the plane and the two liftings cross from opposite sides, notes that type I means no further intersections occur, and concludes that no translation can superimpose the two liftings although they project to the same path (proof lines 1234-1236). core_obligations: One intersection for each path: type I means the lifted path meets each lifted member at most once, so the linear independence criterion applies; since the given path meets one member, its class is independent of that member's class and hence of every member's, so it meets each of them exactly once (proof lines 1254-1259)

For the equality of the counts, take two consecutive liftings of z_1 and the intermediate liftings of the other paths; the lifted w meets them once each in a fixed order, and projecting gives |w cap z_1| = ... = |w cap z_r|.

standard_prerequisites.name: The removability criterion for bypasses
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Invoked inside the counted proof (source lines 5455 and 5452-5465)
standard_prerequisites.use: Shows that the two possible kinds of bypass can always be removed, so the operations may be skipped.

core_obligations: Two geometries: for a hexagonal model the polygon is a triangle and for a rectangular model a parallelogram, and in each case the paths meeting the chosen family are identified as those whose classes are the outer normal vectors of the remaining edges, which by the linear independence criterion do not meet each other on the universal cover (proof lines 5434-5452)

Bypasses are only of two kinds: because the paths meeting the family do not meet each other and the deformed paths of a common slope keep a common slope, every bypass on the universal cover is either a self-intersection of one deformed path or an intersection of two deformed paths of equal slope (proof lines 5454-5463)

Removability: each such edge is a bypass, and two intersecting deformed paths of equal slope meet again, so a non-removable bypass would violate consistency; hence all bypasses introduced by the removal operations can be removed, so those operations may be skipped and the extended deformation coincides with the usual one (proof lines 5463-5466)
proof_roadmap: Reduce to the zig case. The paths z_1,...,z_r have a common slope which is the outer normal vector of an edge of the matching polygon.

Hexagonal case: the polygon is a triangle; the paths meeting the family at zags (resp. zigs) all have one common class, the outer normal vector of the second (resp. third) edge. Rectangular case: the polygon is a parallelogram and the same description holds with the two remaining edges. In both cases paths in the same group do not meet on the universal cover, since the model is isoradial.

Hence every bypass on the universal cover is either a self-intersection of some deformed path or an intersection of two deformed paths of equal slope; such an edge is a bypass, and two deformed paths of equal slope meet again, so a non-removable bypass would break consistency. Therefore all bypasses can be removed and the bypass operation may be skipped.

standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Invoked inside the counted proof (source line 1153)

core_obligations: Set up the fan: order the slopes cyclically using proper ordering, choose a ray whose angle is opposite to the slope of the given path and generic with respect to the slopes, and at each node take the two adjacent zigzag paths around that ray, whose intersection is an edge (proof lines 1099-1110)

Consistency of the selection: applying the same argument at the other endpoint of that edge, proper ordering forces the two edges to coincide, so the selection is well defined and depends only on the parity class of the node (proof lines 1149-1151)
Perfect matching: the cited criteria show that the selected edges form a perfect matching (proof line 1152)

Avoiding the path: type I gives a zigzag path whose slope lies within half a turn of the given slope at each node, which excludes the two selected paths from coinciding with the given one, so the selected edge is not on the path; nodes off the path are immediate (proof lines 1153-1156)
proof_roadmap: Order the slopes of the zigzag paths cyclically (proper ordering) and pick a ray R at angle theta_k + pi + epsilon for the slope of the given path, generic with respect to all slopes.

At each node v take the zigzag paths z'_v and z''_v adjacent to R in the fan at v; by proper ordering they are consecutive and meet in an edge e(v). Applying the same at the other endpoint shows e(v) is independent of the endpoint, so it depends only on the parity class of the node.
By the cited criteria the collection of these edges over one parity class is a perfect matching.

Type I gives a zigzag path of slope within less than a half turn from [z] at each node, which shows z is neither z'_v nor z''_v, so e(v) is not an edge of z; for nodes off z this is immediate. Hence the matching meets z in no edge.

standard_prerequisites.name: The decomposition of a polyhedron as a Minkowski sum of a polytope and a polyhedral cone
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Invoked at the start of the counted proof (source lines 2692-2693)
standard_prerequisites.use: Provides the presentation of the polyhedron used in both inclusions.

standard_prerequisites.name: The description of the dual polyhedron by the inequalities given by the chosen generators
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Established inside the counted proof (source lines 2696-2699)
standard_prerequisites.use: Identifies the dual with the intersection of the half spaces appearing in the generators.

core_obligations: First inclusion: writing the polyhedron as a Minkowski sum, every point of the dual satisfies the inequalities coming from the polytope part by scaling, and satisfies the inequalities from the cone part because otherwise a large multiple of a cone generator would violate the defining inequality of the dual (proof lines 2701-2706)
Reverse inclusion: expanding a point of the polyhedron along the generators and applying the inequalities of the intersection gives the defining inequality of the dual (proof lines 2708-2716)

Involution: one inclusion is immediate from the definitions, and for the reverse one takes a point outside the polyhedron, uses the description as an intersection of half spaces to find a functional violating one of the inequalities, and exhibits a point of the dual pairing with it below minus one, so the point is not in the double dual (proof lines 2718-2725)
proof_roadmap: Write P = Q + C with Q a polytope and C a cone, expanding Q by vertices and C by generators; then P* is the intersection of the half spaces given by those vectors with the prescribed constants.

If v is in P*, scaling the vertex vectors (which lie in P) gives the inequalities with constants -k_i, and a negative value on a cone generator would contradict an element of P having value below -1; hence v lies in the intersection. Conversely, a point of the intersection evaluated on a general element of P, expanded along the generators, is at least -1.

For (ii), P is contained in its double dual by definition; if u is outside P then some inequality of the intersection description fails, and using the normal vector of that inequality (or a positive multiple) produces an element of the dual pairing with u below -1, so u is not in the double dual.
metadata.difficulty_reason: The counted statement says that the dual operation on lattice polytopes containing the origin in their interiors sends such polytopes to polytopes of the same kind and is an involution (author proposition at source lines 2684-2690, label prop_dual_polytope, original numbering Proposition 5.6). The proof (source lines 2692-2726) writes the polyhedron as a Minkowski sum of a polytope and a cone, identifies the dual with the intersection of the half spaces given by the chosen generators, proves the two inclusions of that identification by rescaling the generators and by expanding elements along them, and then proves the involution by exhibiting for a point outside the polyhedron an element of the dual pairing with it below minus one (proof lines 2718-2725). The half space description of the dual is the substance; the single cited entry (Schrijver) is shipped as a verbatim bibliography fragment. H3.

standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Invoked in both parts of the counted proof (source lines 2753 and 2774-2776)
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the transformation whose restriction to the dual polytope is described, and its inverse on each cone of the normal fan.

standard_prerequisites.name: The description of the vertices of a mutated polytope in terms of vertices of the original polytope and of the face
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Invoked inside the counted proof (source lines 2756-2770)
standard_prerequisites.use: Reduces the required inequality to inequalities satisfied on the original polytope.

core_obligations: First inclusion: take a point of the dual polytope, write it as its image under the shear, and check the defining inequality at every vertex of the mutated polytope, splitting into the two cases according to the sign of the pairing of the vertex with the weight vector; in each case the vertex is expressed through vertices of the original polytope and of the face, and the inequality follows from the original dual inequality (proof lines 2756-2771)

Second inclusion: for a point of the dual of the mutated polytope, the cited description of the shear as a unimodular transformation on each cone of the normal fan of the face provides the preimage, which lies in the dual of the original polytope, so the point is the image of a point of that dual (proof lines 2773-2776)
proof_roadmap: Write phi for the shear and Q for the mutated polytope. To show phi(P*) is contained in Q*, take v in P* and test the defining inequality at a vertex u of Q.

If <w,u> is at least zero, u = u_P + <w,u_P> u_F with u_P a vertex of P and u_F a vertex of the face; the inequality follows from <v,u_P> >= -1 and the definition of the minimum. If <w,u> is negative, u - <w,u> u_F lies in P, which gives <v,u> >= -1 + v_min <w,u>, hence the same conclusion.

For the reverse inclusion, the cited discussion describes phi on each maximal cone of the normal fan of the face as a unimodular transformation, so a point of Q* pulled back by the inverse transformation lies in P*.

standard_prerequisites.name: The strong marriage condition as a characterization of non-degeneracy
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Invoked at the start of the counted proof (source line 3954)
standard_prerequisites.use: Reduces non-degeneracy to a matching condition that is preserved when edges are added.

standard_prerequisites.name: The algorithm producing a sub-dimer model satisfying the order condition on the zigzag paths through each edge
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Invoked inside the counted proof (source lines 3977-3978 and 3997-3999)
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the sub-model to which the deformation can be applied and which satisfies the auxiliary condition.

standard_prerequisites.name: The existence of corner matchings adjacent to the chosen paths and of a corner matching disjoint from them
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Invoked inside the counted proof (source lines 4040-4043)
standard_prerequisites.use: Provides the matchings used to build, for each edge, a perfect matching containing it.

core_obligations: First reduction: adding edges preserves the strong marriage condition, so it suffices to prove non-degeneracy for the model obtained by the first three operations (proof lines 3953-3959)

Construction of the auxiliary sub-model: by the cited algorithm one removes edges so that the matching polygon becomes a triangle or a trapezoid, the chosen paths stay type I and the paths through each remaining edge satisfy the stated alternative; hence the sub-model satisfies the auxiliary condition (proof lines 3961-4020)
Second reduction: the deformed model is obtained from the deformation of the sub-model by adding edges, so it suffices to treat that smaller model (proof lines 4022-4027)

Edge-by-edge matchings: for each of the four kinds of edge the proof exhibits a perfect matching containing that edge, using the two adjacent corner matchings and the corner matching disjoint from the chosen paths; the fourth case uses the auxiliary condition to split into sub-cases (proof lines 4029-4093)
proof_roadmap: Since adding edges preserves the strong marriage condition, and the fourth operation only adds edges, it suffices to show that the model obtained from the first three operations is non-degenerate.

Using the algorithm of the cited references, remove edges from the original model so that the matching polygon becomes a triangle or a trapezoid; the chosen paths remain type I and the paths through each edge satisfy (*1) or (*2). Call this sub-model Gamma_sub; it satisfies (*).
Apply the first three operations to Gamma_sub to get Gamma'_sub; the deformed model contains it as a sub-model obtained by adding edges, so it suffices to prove Gamma'_sub non-degenerate.

Prove that for every edge e of Gamma'_sub there is a perfect matching containing it: split the edges into the four kinds (i)-(iv) given in the proof, build the matching explicitly in the first three cases from the corner matchings, and in the fourth case use the condition (*) and the corner matching disjoint from the chosen paths.
